hook: Follow a radio reportage through a city's last dark hour and say what its images mean in plain words.
intro: A radio feature of about 450 words – literary reportage, heard once – about the hour before dawn in a big city. A feature persuades by images, so the questions ask both what happens and what effect the language has. It opens by refuting a cliché in the Konjunktiv I (Wer glaubt, eine Großstadt schlafe nie, der irrt.), follows the reporter through the silent streets, lets a night taxi driver speak in reported speech, and closes by turning back to an ordinary working morning. Listen for the personifications (Die Häuser haben ihre Augen geschlossen.), the similes with wie (gewissenhaft wie Beamte, wie ein Aquarium auf Schienen), the metaphors (eine kleine Insel in einem Meer aus Dunkelheit), and the exact numbers and times, which the questions like to twist.
tips[0].title: Wer glaubt, …, der irrt: the cliché in the Konjunktiv
tips[0].text: The opening names a common belief in the Konjunktiv I (schlafe) and denies it. A question on which idea the feature challenges is answered by that Konjunktiv clause. The same mood later marks the taxi driver’s words as reported (gehöre, könne), while the reporter’s own observations are in the indicative.
tips[0].trap: The refuted belief is not that the city is loud by day – the piece ends by accepting exactly that.
tips[0].check.why: The belief in the Konjunktiv I (sei) is the cliché, and der täuscht sich rejects it.
tips[1].title: Translate each image into plain words
tips[1].text: Effect questions ask what an image does. Personification makes the city a living body (den Atem anzuhalten, Die Stadt atmet wieder aus.); a simile with wie compares openly (wie ein Tuch, wie ein Aquarium auf Schienen); a metaphor says it without wie (Insel, Meer aus Dunkelheit, Wächter). Put each image into a plain sentence – the city is quiet; a few people are awake – then choose the option that matches, not the one that repeats the image’s words.
tips[1].trap: Exaggeration traps turn “nicht leer” into “complete silence” or a few lit windows into “most people work at night”.
tips[1].check.why: It is a personification: the station is pictured as a body holding its breath, which simply means stillness, not people literally holding their breath.
tips[2].title: The closing turn back to the everyday
tips[2].text: Features rarely end on their most poetic image. This one leaves the dawn behind, puts the reporter next to a yawning worker and accepts the city as it usually is. At the end, listen for acceptance rather than complaint.
tips[2].trap: „und warum sollte er auch?“ defends the worker; it is not a reproach.
tips[2].check.why: wie jeden Morgen frames the scene as ordinary routine, accepted rather than criticised or celebrated.
remember[0]: Wer glaubt, …, der irrt → the refuted cliché is the Konjunktiv clause.
remember[1]: Personification, simile (wie), metaphor: translate the image, then answer.
remember[2]: Numbers and times are traps: three nights of searching, found on the fourth; kurz nach vier, gegen halb fünf.
remember[3]: The ending returns to the everyday and accepts it.
exam: Radio features and literary reportage are a C2 exam listening text — and the heart of German public radio on a Sunday morning.
tips[0].check.q: 'Wer meint, auf dem Land sei es immer ruhig, der täuscht sich.' Which idea does the piece challenge?
tips[0].check.options[0]: That the countryside is always quiet
tips[0].check.answer: That the countryside is always quiet
tips[1].check.q: 'Der Bahnhof hält den Atem an.' In plain words:
tips[1].check.options[0]: The station is quiet, as if waiting
tips[1].check.options[1]: People at the station are holding their breath
tips[1].check.options[2]: The station is closed for good
tips[1].check.answer: The station is quiet, as if waiting
tips[2].check.q: A feature ends: 'Der Bäcker gähnt und schiebt die Brötchen in den Ofen, wie jeden Morgen.' What is the tone?
